items.title: Kilmar Ábrego García arrives in Spain, ending Trump deportation battle
items.summary: His deportation to and return from El Salvador became a flashpoint in the debate the US president's immigration agenda.
items.body:
Image source, Getty Images

ByRebecka Pieder

Updated 20 minutes ago

Kilmar Ábrego García, whose deportation last year to El Salvador sparked a bitter deportation battle, is leaving the US for Spain.

He is set to take a commercial flight to the country on Tuesday, according to CBS News, the BBC's US partner.

After the government admitted it had wrongfully sent Ábrego García to his home country, he was returned to the US to face human trafficking charges, which were later dropped. The administration then continued its attempts to send him to other countries, including Uganda and Ghana.

His deportation and return became a flashpoint in the debate over President Donald Trump's immigration agenda.

Ábrego García, who is married to a US citizen and lived in Maryland, came to the US illegally from El Salvador as a teenager.

Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, visited Ábrego García while he was in the notorious Cecot prison in El Salvador in 2025 and advocated for his release.

"A year and a half ago, the Trump Administration wanted to leave Kilmar Ábrego García to rot in a Salvadoran gulag," Van Hollen said in a statement on Tuesday. "Today, Kilmar is travelling to a country of his choice, a free man - unharmed and with dignity."

In a statement, Ábrego García's lawyer said his departure was "temporary" as he had "many options to return to the United States".

"We don't expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritize reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland," the statement said.

"Where he goes from here, where he chooses to settle for the next two years while he waits out the end of this administration, will be his choice, not the administration's choice."

The BBC has contacted the US Department of Homeland Security for comment.

Ábrego García was arrested in 2019 alongside three other men and detained by federal immigration authorities. A judge granted him protection from deportation to El Salvador at the time, citing the risk of persecution by a gang there.

In March 2025, the Trump administration deported him to El Salvador, where he was held in Cecot, a prison known for its harsh conditions. The US Supreme Court then ordered the government to facilitate his return.

The administration admitted that he was deported in error and brought him back to the US where he was set to face human trafficking charges. A federal judge dismissed the case, saying Ábrego García had been charged for political reasons.

For months, he was locked in a battle over deportation with the government.

Ábrego García had repeatedly said he would be willing to be deported to Costa Rica, and the Costa Rican government had agreed to accept him as a refugee and provide him with legal status.

After reports emerged that the administration was considering sending him to Uganda, a judge barred the government from deporting Ábrego García to a third country.

At one point the Trump administration requested that the judge lift the order so that Ábrego García could be deported to Liberia, CBS reported.

items.title: Veteran Nigerian Nollywood actor Pete Edochie dies aged 79
items.summary: Odochie rose to prominence in 1987 after starring in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart.
items.body:
Image source, peteedochie/Instagram

Image caption,

Pete Edochie was one of Africa's most celebrated film stars

ByWycliffe Muia

Updated 43 minutes ago

Veteran Nigerian actor Pete Edochie, one of Africa's most celebrated film stars, has died at the age of 79, his family has announced.

Known for his deep voice, commanding screen presence and memorable use of African proverbs, Edochie became a household name across Africa, often portraying powerful traditional rulers, wealthy businessmen and family patriarchs.

In a statement, his family said Edochie died in the early hours of Wednesday in the south-eastern Nigerian city of Enugu following a prolonged battle with prostate cancer.

Tributes are pouring in from fans and fellow actors, remembering him as a Nollywood legend who helped shape Nigeria's film industry.

Edochie began his career as a broadcaster in 1967 before turning to acting. He rose to prominence in 1987 after starring in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart.

His portrayal of Okonkwo, the proud but troubled Igbo warrior in Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart, earned him international recognition helping establish him as one of Nigeria's most respected actors.

The television series depicted the struggles of an African community as British colonial rule and Christianity began to transform its traditional way of life.

He went on to become one of the most recognisable faces of Nollywood, Nigeria's film industry, which has since grown into one of the world's largest film industries.

Over a career spanning several decades, he appeared in numerous films, including Igodo, Rituals, Billionaire's Club and the 2018 romantic comedy Lionheart.

His contribution to the arts was recognised in 2003 when he received one of Nigeria's national honours, the Member of the Order of the Niger (MON).

He also received several other accolades during his career, including the Industry Merit Award at the Africa Magic Viewers' Choice Awards.

In recent years, his distinctive facial expressions, witty remarks and memorable scenes from his films found a new generation of admirers through viral social media memes.

"As we mourn this painful loss, we pray that Almighty God grants his gentle soul eternal rest and gives the entire family the fortitude to bear this irreparable loss," a statement shared on Instagram by his son Leo said.

Enugu State Governor Peter Mbah said Edochie's death was a huge loss to Nigeria, praising the actor for introducing international audiences to Igbo traditions and inspiring younger performers.

"Pete Edochie was more than an accomplished actor, he was an institution," Mbah said.

The Actors Guild of Nigeria (AGN) president, Abubakar Yakubu, described Edochie as a "father figure" in the entertainment industry, saying his influence would be felt for generations to come.

Edochie had spoken publicly about his deteriorating health during a visit to Ghana in October, saying he was struggling to walk and experiencing swelling in parts of his body.

He is survived by his wife, Josephine, and their six children, including fellow Nollywood actors Yul and Linc Edochie.

items.title: Russia's own figures show it has lost nearly 500,000 people in Ukraine war
items.summary: Leaked data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia.
items.body:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images

Image caption,

Russia does not provide numbers of its fallen soldiers

ByOlga Ivshina, BBC Russian and Yaroslava Kiryukhina, BBC Russian

At least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, according to Russian government statistics analysed by the BBC.

The leaked Rosstat data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia, and show the high cost paid in human life in a war that Vladimir Putin had assumed would last only days but is now almost five years old.

BBC Russian has had access to more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, after a hack by Belarusian group Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow.

Russia's statistics agency admitted to a cyber-attack, but denied any protected information had been leaked.

Together with independent Russian outlet Mediazona, BBC Russian has compared the Rosstat data with its own list of confirmed military deaths, pulled from open sources since the start of the invasion, and it has found matches for 90% of the records.

The records show that 65% of 18 to 24 year-olds in Russia who lost their lives in 2025 died in the war. For those aged 25-34 the number was 59%. Only among 45 to 54 year-olds does cardiovascular disease claim more Russian lives than the conflict.

The data also reveal the extent of losses in specific areas of Ukraine. Some 20,000 Russian soldiers died fighting for control of 10 Ukrainian villages whose combined pre-war population was 12,000.

During the fight for one small village called Andriivka, south of the town of Bakhmut in Donetsk region, 1,122 Russians lost their lives. Before the war 74 people lived there.

Russia does not give public figures for losses sustained since the war began in February 2022. And two years ago Rosstat stopped publishing data of deaths from external causes, which was used to gauge the extent of military losses.

For example, only 70% of deaths we have established of soldiers from the occupied regions of Donetsk and Luhansk in eastern Ukraine who fought in the Russian army were accounted for in the Rosstat files.

How we came to a figure near half a million

The Rosstat dataset contains no names but does include ages, places of residence, places of death and also circumstances of death.

We have filtered the records first by location, leaving only Ukraine as well as Russian border regions that saw incursions by the Ukrainian army.

Next, we identified 425,174 entries explicitly indicating a military-related cause of death, such as explosions or shrapnel during combat operations.

As this count could include civilians, we filtered out women as well as men outside the 18-65 age group. And if someone lived and died in the four Ukrainian regions occupied by Russia, we excluded them as a possible civilian – unless he had a record of military service attached to his entry.

Another 14,093 entries were identified by looking at employment, and 51,067 were recorded in the database as deceased on the basis of a court ruling. This often happens when a soldier goes missing in a combat zone for more than six months and their body has not been recovered.

Again, we filtered out civilians by only counting deaths in the war zones in Ukraine and Russia.

BBC Russian's own detailed records of Russian losses has reached 290,012, verified together with Mediazona from official reports, social media, new memorials and graves. The actual death toll is likely to be higher, as not all deaths are reported publicly.

Overall, the Rosstat dataset confirms the trends that we have observed with our own count.

According to BBC Russian's analysis of the leaked files, in the first year of the war the average age of those killed was 34. By 2025, as prisoners and contract soldiers entered the ranks, it had risen to 40 (38 according to our own list).

Some of Russia's poorest regions in Eastern Siberia account for a disproportionately large share of the losses. Men from Tyva, Buryatia and Zabaykalsky Krai are 20-25 times more likely to die in the war than residents of the biggest cities of Moscow and St Petersburg.

Image source, AFP via Getty Images

In most regions, the distribution of deaths based on Rosstat data differs from that in the BBC's list by just a few tenths of a percentage point.

At least 5,017 foreigners are among those who died fighting for Russia, according to our analysis of the Rosstat files, including 1,031 Uzbeks and 720 Tajiks. We have left out Ukrainians from this count to avoid including civilians.

This is a conservative estimate as dual nationals are listed as Russians in the database, and there is no reference to North Koreans who died repelling the Ukrainian incursion into Russia in 2024.

The BBC identified 2,304 North Korean soldiers who died there by analysing satellite imagery and official photographs of a newly built memorial in Pyongyang.

The leaked Russian statistics may not be complete but taken in conjunction with BBC Russian's own work they are significant. Military experts estimate that the BBC's figure of 290,012, gleaned from open sources, may account for 45-55% of the true death toll – ranging from 527,295 to 644,471.

In the context of a war that has lasted four years and 10 months, these are high numbers for Russia, when compared with the Soviet war in Afghanistan that ended in 1989.

Ukrainian losses were last put at about 50,000 by President Volodymyr Zelensky in July 2026, but another list based on open sources by the anonymous UA Losses website puts the figure at 115,952.

Additional reporting by Ilya Barabanov

items.title: South Africa's Ramaphosa wins court battle over impeachment threat
items.summary: The break-in happened in 2020, when thieves allegedly stole bundles of US dollar bills hidden inside a sofa at the farm.
items.body:
Image source, Gallo via Getty Images

Image caption,

President Cyril Ramaphosa has faced calls to resign over his handling of the "Farmgate" scandal

ByKhanyisile Ngcobo

Reporting fromJohannesburg

Updated 2 hours ago

South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has won a legal battle to overturn a report that found he may have a case to answer over the theft of large sums of cash from his private farm.

In 2022, an independent panel said Ramaphosa may have committed serious misconduct relating to the theft of $580,000 (£443,000), hidden in a sofa, at his Phala Phala game farm in the Limpopo province. He denied any wrongdoing.

Ramaphosa challenged the findings of the report in court after the Constitutional Court ruled that parliament had violated the constitution by blocking moves to impeach him.

The Western Cape high court ruled that the panel's report was unlawful and set it aside "in its entirety".

In its judgment, the court said the panel, appointed by parliament to investigate the allegations against Ramaphosa, had "misconstrued its function, the nature of the inquiry it was to conduct and the recommendation it was required to make".

"It went beyond its lawful remit ... and made several material errors of law. [Therefore] the report of the independent panel ... is declared unlawful and is reviewed and set aside in its entirety," Judge Nolwazi Mabindla-Boqwana said.

The court also declared unlawful the steps taken by parliament in relation to the report.

The ruling effectively removes the basis for the parliamentary impeachment process against Ramaphosa, although opposition parties have indicated they intend to challenge the decision.

The scandal, dubbed "Farmgate" by local media, has has dogged Ramaphosa since it emerged in 2022, when former spy chief Arthur Fraser reported the matter to police in a dossier.

Fraser, an ally of former President Jacob Zuma, accused Ramaphosa of concealing the theft from the police and tax authorities.

The break-in took place in 2020, when thieves allegedly stole bundles of US dollar bills hidden inside a sofa at the farm.

Image source, Gallo via Getty Images

Image caption,

Opposition parties, pictured above, have been vocal in their call for the president to account for his role in the saga

Earlier this month, two people were found guilty of the theft.

Ramaphosa confirmed that a robbery had taken place but said the money had been from the legitimate sale of buffalo from his livestock business.

Several investigations cleared him of any wrongdoing, but parliament began an impeachment proceedings in 2022 and appointed an independent panel to investigate the allegations.

The panel made a series of damaging findings, including that there was "substantial doubt about the legitimacy of the source of the currency that was stolen".

It also concluded that Ramaphosa "has a case to answer".

Ramaphosa initially challenged the report in court but withdrew his application after parliament voted against adopting its findings.

He revived the legal challenge again in May this year after the Constitutional Court, the country's highest court, ruled that parliament had acted unconstitutionally by blocking moves to impeach him.

It ordered parliament to refer the report to an impeachment committee.

In his latest challenge, Ramaphosa argued that the panel had "misconceived its mandate, misjudged the information placed before it and misinterpreted the four charges advanced against me".

The Western Cape High Court's ruling could bring the current impeachment process to an end, unless parliament successfully challenges the decision.

If they do, and the appeal is successful, the parliamentary committee would be able to examine the charges against the president and make a recommendation.

If the committee recommends impeachment, parliament would have to vote on whether to remove him from office. This would require the support of at least two-thirds majority in parliament.

Ramaphosa's Africa National Congress (ANC) has enough parliamentary seats to block such a move.

He is the first president to face impeachment proceedings under the rules introduced in 2018.

items.title: Colombian police storm supermarket to free 20 held hostage for 17 hours
items.summary: One gunman was killed in the operation to free around 20 shoppers and employees after a 17-hour hostage ordeal.
items.body:
Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images

Image caption,

Relatives of those being held hostage spent anxious hours as the situation unfolded

ByVanessa Buschschlüter

Latin America online editor

Colombian security forces have freed around 20 shoppers and employees who had been held hostage for about 17 hours at a supermarket in the city of Cartagena.

Gunmen had stormed into the building at 08:00 (13:00 GMT) on Tuesday after what local media said was a failed attempt of robbing an armoured car carrying money and valuables.

They held those inside at gunpoint while trying to negotiate their getaway.

With the situation becoming ever more intense as the day progressed, Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella gave the green light for special forces and police to launch a daring operation to free the hostages, in which one gunman was killed.

Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images

Image caption,

Around 20 people were still being held hostage when the security forces moved in

Residents living near the supermarket reported hearing explosions as the security forces moved into the building.

Police later confirmed that officers had used stun grenades to overpower the hostage takers.

De la Espriella described it as "an extraordinary joint operation", which he said had been carried out "flawlessly".

He flew into the northern city to oversee the operation.

In footage released since then, he can be seen speaking into a walkie-talkie and carrying a handgun strapped to his side.

Speaking after the successful rescue of the hostages, he said that the gunmen had been given the chance to hand themselves in, which they had refused.

Earlier in the day, the men had freed 10 of their hostages, among them elderly women.

But they continued to hold around 20, even as a police helicopter hovered above and special forces erected a perimeter around the building.

Local media said that as well as demanding safe passage out of the supermarket, the gunmen also demanded nearly $2m (£1.5m) and armoured vehicles.

According to President De la Espriella, they had no political affiliations but had taken the hostages once their plan to rob an armoured car carrying money had been foiled.

"It's not that a terrorist group carried out a kidnapping - no, these are criminals who were caught off guard, had no way out, and then kidnapped a group of people," he said.

Photos taken during the rescue operation show armed soldiers inside the building while people are kneeling with their hands behind their heads.

items.title: Huawei found guilty of stealing US trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
items.summary: The verdict follows a months-long trial in New York.
items.body:
Image source, REUTERS/Jane Rosenberg

Image caption,

Defence lawyer Brian Heberlig makes closing arguments at the Huawei Technologies trial at Brooklyn federal court on November 17.

ByRachel Clun

Business reporter

Updated 8 minutes ago

Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark case in the US.

In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage.

Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation.

Huawei said, external the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis", adding that it would "take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests".

Jurors in a Brooklyn court found Huawei guilty of 10 out of 12 counts, which included conspiracy to violate US sanctions.

However, the jury declined to convict Huawei of the racketeering conspiracy charge, which required members to find the firm acted like a criminal enterprise.

Federal prosecutors first announced the charges against Huawei in 2019, after the dramatic arrest in late 2018 of senior executive Meng Wanzhou in Canada.

Meng, also known as Cathy Meng, was held for three years in Canada before she was released to return to China through a deal with US prosecutors.

During closing arguments last week, assistant US attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors Huawei spent 20 years doing whatever it took to expand its business, including lying to banks about its business dealings in Iran and stealing technology secrets from rival firms to ensure it had a competitive edge.

"For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft," US Attorney General Todd Blanche said in statement, external.

"Thanks to the work of the FBI and our federal prosecutors, those who engaged in these criminal activities will be held accountable."

However, defence attorney Brian Heberlig said it was by dint of hard work that Huawei's business had expanded with operations in 170 countries and more than 200,000 staff.

Following the verdict, Heberlig told the BBC that Huawei was gratified that the jury had rejected the racketeering charge.

"The RICO [Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act] count that alleged that Huawei was a corrupt organisation, with a corporate culture and policy of committing crime. That was, in our view, a significant overreach, and the jury soundly rejected it," he said.

"Of course, we have mixed emotions about the rest of the verdict ... [we] thought that Huawei was deserving of acquittals across the board."

Sentencing is planned for September 2027. Heberlig said there will be "significant advocacy" to achieve the lowest sentence possible. Following that, he said he fully expects Huawei to appeal.

"If I know Huawei, that fight will continue, and the company's not going to rest until it's pursued every last argument it can through appeal, and hopefully, ultimately toward vindication," he said.

items.title: Zimbabwe issues arrest warrant for Robert Mugabe's son over missed court date
items.summary: The son of Zimbabwe's late former President Robert Mugabe has faced multiple legal troubles in the recent past.
items.body:
Image source, Gallo Images via Getty Images

Image caption,

Bellarmine Chatunga is the youngest son of Robert Mugabe and his second wife, Grace Mugabe

ByBasillioh Rukanga

A Zimbabwean court has issued an arrest warrant for Bellarmine Chatunga Mugabe, the youngest son of the country's late former president Robert Mugabe, after he failed to appear in court.

Mugabe was arrested earlier this month alongside four others over assault allegations on a police officer during an investigation into the suspected smuggling of luxury vehicles.

The group subsequently faced charges of robbery and malicious damage to property. They have yet to enter pleas.

They were granted bail on 6 November and were due back in court on Tuesday. However, Mugabe failed to attend. His co-accused, an aide and three security guards appeared and were remanded until 10 December.

Prosecutors allege that Mugabe and the others assaulted an investigating officer using their hands and broomsticks.

The officer's phone was allegedly taken and smashed on the ground, while one of the accused is said to have seized the officer's loaded pistol.

Bellarmine Chatunga is the youngest son of Robert Mugabe and his second wife, Grace Mugabe.

Robert Mugabe ruled Zimbabwe for 37 years before being forced from power in 2017, aged 93, following a military intervention. He died in 2019.

His son has attracted public attention in recent years over a series of legal troubles and his high-profile lifestyle.

Last month, he admitted to drug-related charges involving the possession of cannabis.

In April, he was deported from neighbouring South Africa after pleading guilty to pointing a firearm and being in the country illegally. He had been arrested following the shooting of a 23-year-old man at his home.

In 2023, he was arrested in Harare, Zimbabwe's capital, over allegations that he damaged property and spat at a police officer during a party.

He was later freed after reaching an out-of-court settlement with the complainant, who was a friend.

items.title: Two children among six dead after plane crash off Mississippi coast
items.summary: Divers found the bodies of four adults and two boys, aged 8 and 10, in the fuselage, the US Coast Guard said.
items.body:
Image source, Getty Images

ByHarriet Whitehead

Six people, including two children, have been found dead after a plane crashed off the coast of Mississippi on Tuesday, the US Coast Guard says.

The Cessna 210 was on its way from New Orleans to Fort Myers, Florida, according to the flight tracking website FlightAware. Air traffic control lost touch with it at about 15:45 (21:45 GMT) and it later went down in the Gulf of Mexico between Pascagoula and Horn Island, officials said.

Divers found the bodies of four adults and two boys, aged 8 and 10, in the fuselage, said Coast Guard spokesperson Juan Ros.

Rescuers spent hours searching for the group and initially only found three life jackets, a life raft and the plane's cabin floating on the water, he said.

Cmdr Trevor Blount, the Coast Guard rescue mission co-ordinator, said: "While this is not the outcome any of us had hoped for, we are grateful for the strong interagency co-ordination that enabled us to swiftly locate those aboard the aircraft and provide closure to their families."

items.title: Close-up images to be revealed of asteroid deliberately hit to test ability to protect Earth
items.summary: The mission is studying an asteroid deliberately knocked off course by a colliding spacecraft.
items.body:
Image source, ESA

Image caption,

The Hera spacecraft will study the 150m-wide (490ft) asteroid called Dimorphos

ByRebecca Morelle , Alison Francis and Tony Jolliffe, BBC News Science

A spacecraft has arrived at an asteroid to investigate the damage caused by an unprecedented cosmic crash.

It what may sound like the plot of a disaster movie, Nasa's Dart spacecraft deliberately smashed into the space rock in 2022 to knock it off course.

The Nasa craft was obliterated on impact. Four years on, a European Space Agency (ESA) mission, called Hera, is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision - with the first images set to be released later on Wednesday.

The asteroid poses no threat, instead this was the first ever test of our planetary defences to see what action we could take if a space rock was heading for our planet.

"Hera is a sort of Inspector Columbo going back to the crash scene to investigate what is the outcome of this impact," said Patrick Michel, principal investigator of ESA's Hera mission.

Image source, NASA/Johns Hopkins APL

Image caption,

This was the last image from Dart before it crashed into Dimorphos in 2022

The crash test focussed on a pair of asteroids: a larger one called Didymos - about 730m (2,400ft) wide - which is orbited by a smaller rock called Dimorphos, about 150m (490ft) wide.

The Dart spacecraft targeted Dimorphos, hurtling into the rock at 22,000km per hour (14,000mph). Images beamed back showed the asteroid's rocky surface coming ever closer until the feed cut out on impact.

It was such a big smash-up that the trail of debris, measuring about 10,000km long (6,200 miles), was spotted by telescopes on Earth and in space.

The crash showed it was possible to change the path of the smaller asteroid.

Before the collision it took Dimorphos 11 hours and 55 minutes to orbit around Didymos. After the Dart crash, the duration of its orbit had shrunk by about 33 minutes.

But the arrival of the second spacecraft, Hera, will help scientists to answer many more questions.

"Dart exploded in the asteroid, and therefore we don't have the information of what is its final state," explained Michel.

"The impact could have left a crater - and if it is the case, we need to understand the size and the depth. Or [the impact] may have entirely reshaped the asteroid."

Image source, NASA/Hubble Space Telescope

Image caption,

A 10,000km-long (6,200 miles) debris trail was spotted by the Hubble Space Telescope

The Hera mission will spend the next year studying Dimorphos, and take a look at Didymos too.

The spacecraft is packed with instruments, and it also has two small shoe-boxed sized satellites onboard, which can study the impact site up close, and then later land on the asteroid.

A key task is to measure the mass of Dimorphos, to work out how effective the spacecraft's shove was.

This information would be vital if we ever spotted a space rock that was on a collision course with Earth.

"It would help us to predict what would happen if we had to hit another asteroid," said Prof Simon Green, a planetary scientist who is on Hera's science team.

"We [could] measure its properties and say: 'Well, we need this mass of spacecraft, travelling at this speed, this early, in order to deflect it enough so that it misses the Earth'."

Image source, ESA

Image caption,

Hera has already sent back an image of Didymos with Dimorphos in the background

Asteroids pose a significant threat to our planet.

The biggest, which measure more than a kilometre across, could cause global devastation. But medium-sized asteroids around the same dimensions as Dimorphos could wipe out a city.

"We all know what happened to the dinosaurs, right? And we don't want that to happen to us," said Carolyn Ernst, Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, who works on both the Dart and Hera missions.

"The good news for us is that there are far fewer potential threats out there in the Solar System than there were millions of years ago. But there are objects out there."

She said the biggest asteroids have been spotted, and none are heading to Earth.

"The smallest stuff isn't too much of a threat because our atmosphere protects us," she added.

"But there's a size range in the middle where we don't know where all of them are, and it could, if impacted, cause problems for humanity. And if we can find out about that and know about that, well, we sure as heck would want to try to stop that."

Image source, ESA

Image caption,

Hera has two small satellites onboard to study the asteroid up close

Scientists want to gather as much intelligence as they can about space rocks - to make us as well equipped as possible to deal with whatever the Universe throws at us.

A new mission is launching in 2027 to track potentially hazardous asteroids: a space telescope called the Near-Earth Object (NEO) Surveyor.

There are also more visits planned to asteroids, including to one called Apophis, which is about 450m (1,480ft) long.

Apophis was discovered in 2004 and it was initially thought it might hit the Earth as early as 13 April 2029.

But now scientists understand its orbit better, and say it won't hit us for at least the next 100 years. Instead of a crash in 2029, it will fly just 32,000km (20,000 miles) above our surface.

This will give scientists the rare chance to study a space rock up-close.

Two spacecraft will head to Apophis, including Nasa's Osiris-Apex (which previously grabbed a sample from another asteroid called Bennu) and Ramses, a joint mission between ESA and the Japanese Space Agency (JAXA).

Figure caption,

ByRachel Clun and Michael Race, Business reporters

items.title: Solomon Islands ends controversial security pact with China for Australian treaty
items.summary: Solomon Islands leader Matthew Wale said his country would no longer be a point of regional uncertainty.
items.body:
Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

Australia and the Solomon Islands have signed a new treaty on security and economics

ByHelen Davidson

Reporting fromSydney

The Solomon Islands has signed a "historic" treaty with Australia, after reportedly telling China it was ending a controversial security pact signed in 2022.

At a press conference in Canberra on Wednesday, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Solomon Islands counterpart Matthew Wale said the new treaty would ensure that Australia was the Pacific nation's "security partner of choice".

In 2022 the Solomon Islands, then under the leadership of now-Opposition Leader Manasseh Sogavare, signed a security and policing pact with Beijing.

There were fears the pact gave China a crucial military and strategic foothold in the Pacific amid a battle for influence in the region with the US.

On Tuesday, Australian media outlets reported that Honiara had told Beijing it would not renew the pact, understood to be expiring in April 2027.

Wale told reporters on Wednesday there were "ongoing discussions" with China but he was "unable to talk about" the pact, because of a non-disclosure agreement.

He said the treaty with Australia provided a reset after several years in which the Solomon Islands had been a point of "uncertainty and doubt in the region".

"Those days are done, gone," Wale said.

Albanese said the treaty would strengthen the two countries' security partnership.

"Backing our Pacific neighbours is an investment in Australia's own security and our own prosperity."

"We'll do that in a way that completely respects Solomon Islands sovereignty and its right to make its own decisions."

On Tuesday China's foreign ministry spokesman, Guo Jiukan, did not confirm or deny that the pact had been terminated.

"There is no element of geopolitical rivalry or bloc confrontation in cooperation between China and Pacific island countries, including the Solomon Islands," Guo said.

The pact was never publicly released, but leaked excerpts revealed it gave China extensive involvement in security and policing including deploying its own officers to the Solomon Islands, and allowed it to establish a quasi military base.

It was a "massive coup" for Beijing, said Lowy Institute Research Fellow, Dr Connor Graham, but its unprecedented scale sparked alarm in the Pacific and the West.

Wednesday's treaty had delivered "an enormous win for Canberra", and "closes the loop" on a series of security deals Canberra signed with Pacific nations in the wake of the Solomons-China pact.

"That [China pact] was the thing that put fear in the hearts of diplomats in Washington and Canberra," he told the BBC.

William Yang, the International Crisis Group's Senior Analyst for North East Asia, said the end of China's "flagship" Pacific deal and the signing of the new treaty also reaffirmed the Pacific's "longstanding consensus-based decision-making model, especially in the security space".

Under the new treaty, the Solomon Islands commits to prior consultation with Australia on critical infrastructure and to ensure any security cooperations are with Pacific Islands Forum members. China is a dialogue partner but not a member of the forum.

Honiara also commits to its sensitive infrastructure remaining "free from militarisation, any form of foreign interference or unauthorised access", and to not permit its territory to be used for any foreign military or security base.

The Solomons will receive support for its free education system and sports programs, improved visa arrangements, and support for the expansion of affordable and renewable energy and infrastructure development.

Earlier this week the ABC reported the package promised more than A$980m (£460.7m, $648,000) in additional funding, citing leaked text messages. The BBC has not independently verified the text messages.

Wale visited Australia to sign the treaty, accompanied by two dozen Solomons MPs. He and Albanese said the size of the delegation demonstrated that the treaty had strong support from the country's parliament, after years of political instability - largely driven by disagreement over the country's relationship with China.

items.title: Lies, a disguise and surfboard bags: How a jealous Sydney policeman tried to cover up double murder
items.summary: Beau Lamarre was on Wednesday found guilty of murdering his ex Jesse Baird, and Baird's new partner Luke Davies.
items.body:
Image source, NSW Supreme Court

Image caption,

Thousands of hours of CCTV footage helped convict Beau Lamarre

ByHelen Livingstone

Sydney

It was just after 09:00 on a warm February morning when CCTV picked up a man dressed as an UberEats rider hovering on a sidewalk in one of Sydney's wealthiest neighbourhoods.

He dawdled for around 20 minutes, "steeling himself for what he was about to do" prosecutors say, before disappearing out of sight. Minutes later another CCTV camera captured the sound of gunshots ringing out.

Former police officer Beau Lamarre, 31, was on Wednesday found guilty of murdering his former partner Jesse Baird, a TV presenter, and Luke Davies, Baird's new partner, with his work-issued gun.

In February 2024, the bloodied belongings of Baird and Davies were found in a skip in the suburb of Cronulla, sparking a frantic search for the couple. It culminated in the discovery of their bodies on a rural property, partially buried beneath sticks and debris.

Image source, Supplied: Jesse Baird

Image caption,

Luke Davies (left) and Jesse Baird had been dating only months when they were gunned down

During a two-month trial filled with at-times extraordinary testimony and a wealth of CCTV evidence, the court heard Lamarre had planned his crime over months.

Jurors watched CCTV of the then police officer purchasing a surfboard bag in which to put Baird's body, after casually sizing it up against a friend in the shop, and heard from a stream of former friends and colleagues who testified that Lamarre asked them for advice about everything from mobile phone signals to where he could buy a gun.

One recounted the chilling moment Lamarre told her that if he were ever to murder someone, he would leave their belongings in a dumpster and hide the body in bushland where they would never be found.

"What would you do if I told you I killed somebody? Would you help me hide the body?" he asked, according to her testimony.

Later, Lamarre asked for help in covering up the killings; his friends - none of whom have been implicated - say they began receiving panicked calls and odd requests from him.

One told the court Lamarre persuaded her to go for a drive in the country, during which he tried to dispose of the bodies at the family farm of a man he'd met on a dating app. Over the speakers, he played Taylor Swift's No Body, No Crime.

Dark infatuation

Baird, 26, and Lamarre - a one-time celebrity blogger who also had his own swimwear line on the side of his police work - met in a nightclub in October 2022. For Lamarre, it quickly became an infatuation, but for Baird, an AFL referee and former Network Ten presenter, the relationship appeared to be casual.

After discovering in April 2023 that Lamarre had gone through messages on his phone, and unfollowed other men on his Instagram account, Baird broke it off.

But Lamarre's obsession only grew. He watched Baird having sex with another man through his bedroom window, broke into his house multiple times, deleting contacts on his phone and turning on location settings so that he could engineer meetings with the TV presenter.

On one occasion Baird woke up to find Lamarre in his bedroom; not realising who it was, he chased him down the street. Lamarre was also convicted of aggravated break and enter over that incident on Wednesday.

Prosecutor Brett Hatfield said Baird was "oblivious to the accused's scheming and manipulations", and the pair briefly rekindled the relationship before Baird ended it definitively in November.

He'd discovered Lamarre had, again, been accessing his phone and had attempted to ward off a love rival by pretending to have received flowers from Baird.

'The beginning of the plan for murder'

Image source, EPA-EFE/REX/Shutterstock

Image caption,

Beau Lamarre pictured at the annual Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras parade in Sydney in 2020

His pride wounded, Hatfield said Lamarre's thoughts turned to a "darker place": "revenge".

He asked an old friend if her ex-partner could get him a gun: "This was the beginning of the plan for the murder," the prosecutor said.

In the months leading up to the killings, Lamarre bought a burner phone, a motorcycle helmet, and practised shooting in the woods. On holiday with a friend in Bali in January 2024 he tried to buy a silencer.

While his murder plans percolated, he also began lashing out with petty acts of malice, prosecutors said, such as putting water in the fuel tank of Baird's car.

But at the same time as he plotted, Lamarre was still trying to win his ex back.

On one occasion he pressured a friend to send Baird a 1,600-word message he had himself composed, claiming that he had cancer, and may need to have his arm amputated.

Under questioning in court, he said a naturopath he couldn't remember the name of had diagnosed him with "a form of sporadic cancer".

By the end of 2023, Baird had met and hit it off with Davies, 29. "It was early days but they were both smitten with each other," his mother, Helen Baird, told the court. He sent her a picture of the pair at a Pink concert. "I just sent a big love heart and said 'I'm so happy for both of you'."

Image source, Supplied: Jesse Baird

Image caption,

Jesse Baird and Luke Davies at the Pink concert shortly before they were killed

Early on the morning of 19 February, Lamarre picked up a hire car he had asked his mother to rent and drove to Baird's home. After waiting several hours for Baird's housemates to leave, while disguised as an UberEats driver, he let himself in with a key he had copied.

Lamarre told the court he had been at Baird's home to pick up some belongings, including a A$25,000 (US$16,500, £12,600) Cartier ring, and had disguised himself to avoid the embarrassment of being recognised if anyone was home.

He claimed he let himself in when no one answered the door, and the two men were killed in separate struggles. He argued that Baird had been holding a knife and the first shot was fired to disarm him, and the second by accident. Davies shot himself when he grabbed the gun, Lamarre said.

But prosecutors told the jury Baird was shot in the back and then once again through his temple as he lay gravely wounded on the kitchen floor.

The evidence, Hatfield said, pointed to one thing only: "an execution".

Davies was then shot through a bedroom door as he tried to call emergency services. The court heard the panic in his voice as the seconds-long call was replayed before it dropped out.

Covering tracks

After that, Lamarre set about trying to hide the evidence of what Hatfield called his "brazen and shocking murders".

One of his first actions was to call a friend. He testified Lamarre confessed he had "killed people" and asked him to take a day off work "to help him clean up his mess".

Later Lamarre pretended the call was a joke, saying, "Did you like my Oscar performance? Got you".

Meanwhile, Lamarre went to a DIY store to purchase mops, bleach and bin bags. After returning to Baird's house to clean up, he left the bodies wrapped in surfboard bags and tarpaulins in the courtyard.

Baird had been set to move out that week, and Lamarre used Baird's phone to reassure his housemates he had hired an Airtasker to move his belongings, adding, "I might be flying to Perth tonight".

Baird's housemates quickly spotted the surfboard bags when they returned home, snapping a photograph tendered in court which showed "red liquid" seeping out.

"I thought it was rusted water from the outdoor furniture," one of the women said.

The surfboard bags were gone the next morning.

Image source, NSW Supreme Court

Image caption,

Lamarre was captured on CCTV sizing up a surfboard bag in the days before the murders

Lamarre had hired a van, and over the next two days made more trips to the DIY store and a sports shop to buy gumboots, a wheelbarrow, bigger surfboard bags and 10kg weights. He squeezed in a hospital appointment for a minor procedure and paused for a sushi date with a friend, CCTV showing him laughing and eating as the bodies lay in the back of his van.

On 21 February, he picked up another friend in the van for what she thought was lunch.

There were blue tarps in the back and it smelled "lemony", she told the court. She "wasn't allowed to put the windows up or turn the aircon off" as they motored towards Goulburn, 200km southwest of Sydney, stopping only at another DIY store, where he asked her to buy an angle grinder.

His friend told the court she remembers Lamarre playing No Body, No Crime at some point: "It's a very niche song."

Arriving at a farm owned by a Hinge date's family, Lamarre used the angle grinder to cut through a padlock, making his way to a dam where he unsuccessfully tried to sink the bodies.

It was now late at night and he drove his friend, by this time upset and confused, home before returning to retrieve the bodies. He then left them in the van, parked in Sydney overnight, before driving once more to Goulburn, where he dumped the bodies near a monastery.

Later that day he visited another friend, telling her to look up the definition of schizophrenia and asking whether he could use her hose, because "there was a bit of blood he had to scrub off" the hired van, the court heard.

Lamarre faces life in prison

Image source, Getty

Image caption,

The deaths of Baird and Davies triggered an outpouring of horror in Sydney

By this time police were closing in, and on 23 February Lamarre went to turn himself in at Bondi police station. On the way, he called a police helpline.

"I've been bullied by multiple New South Wales police force members," he told the woman on the other end of the line. "All this stress and trauma and psychological abuse and trauma - did I say trauma already? - has caused me to not sleep, get anxious, it's caused me to have some symptoms of schizophrenia."

"Actually sorry, you know what, can you just... delete that whole thing. We'll just keep it short and sweet."

He wasn't sure when he'd be back to work, he said. Shortly afterwards he was arrested and charged with murder, and the bodies of Baird and Davies were found four days later.

Lamarre's lawyer John Stratton insisted he'd acted in self-defence and had "panicked" realising how the scene would look to outsiders.

The former police officer did plenty of "foolish" and "unusual" things - "He was, it's fair to say, a poorly behaved boyfriend," Stratton said - but that did not make him a murderer.

Ultimately, however, the jury was not convinced and took just over an hour to convict him. He will be sentenced in March and faces life in prison.

One of his first actions was to call a friend. He testified Lamarre confessed he had "killed people" and asked him to take a day off work "to help him clean up his mess".
Later Lamarre pretended the call was a joke, saying, "Did you like my Oscar performance? Got you".

Meanwhile, Lamarre went to a DIY store to purchase mops, bleach and bin bags. After returning to Baird's house to clean up, he left the bodies wrapped in surfboard bags and tarpaulins in the courtyard.
Baird had been set to move out that week, and Lamarre used Baird's phone to reassure his housemates he had hired an Airtasker to move his belongings, adding, "I might be flying to Perth tonight".

Lamarre had hired a van, and over the next two days made more trips to the DIY store and a sports shop to buy gumboots, a wheelbarrow, bigger surfboard bags and 10kg weights. On 21 February, he picked up another friend in the van for what she thought was lunch.

By this time police were closing in, and on 23 February Lamarre went to turn himself in at Bondi police station. On the way, he called a police helpline.

items.title: Thomas Markle charged in US for possessing child sex abuse images
items.summary: The FBI arrested Markle on 6 November after a search of a storage unit he had allegedly rented in Los Angeles uncovered the abuse material.
items.body:
Image source, Pinellas County Sheriff's Office

BySareen Habeshian

Reporting fromLos Angeles

Updated 3 hours ago

Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex has been indicted by a federal grand jury in Los Angeles for possessing child sex abuse images.

Markle, who remains in custody in Florida, allegedly possessed materials that include at least one image involving a prepubescent minor and a minor under 12 years old, court documents filed in California show.

The 82-year-old has denied possessing images of child sex abuse. He is expected to be arraigned in Los Angeles in the coming weeks.

Last week, a judge in Florida declared Prince Harry's father-in-law mentally competent to stand trial.

The FBI arrested Markle on 6 November at an elderly care home in Florida on a single federal charge of possessing child sexual abuse material. He now faces two counts.

US attorney Bill Essayli said Markle faces a maximum of 20 years in prison on each count if convicted.

His arrest came after a search of a storage unit he had allegedly rented in Los Angeles for almost two decades uncovered the abuse material.

Markle was initially released on conditional bail but was then ordered to stay in jail pending trial after allegedly removing a location monitoring device.

In the indictment, filed by the US Attorney's Office in the Central District of California, Markle is accused of knowingly possessing 35mm film negatives on 30 October and 4 November that contained child sexual abuse materials.

The US Attorney's Office said that during both instances Markle allegedly knew the images contained such materials.

Inside the storage units, federal agents found two images that depict an adult man - whom a witness identified as Markle - with an underage child, the US attorney's office said.

They also alleged that a third image appears to depict a child in a room believed to be part of a motel chain in the Philippines. Markle moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and he lived in Cebu until May.

"The affidavit also describes additional photographs that appear to show Markle with children in various stages of undress," prosecutors said.

items.title: Trump's rescue of Nvidia's Huang brings political risks
items.summary: The US president's intercession to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang has inextricably linked their fates.
items.body:
Figure caption,

Trump boosts Nvidia boss return but are US politicians on board?

ByAnthony Zurcher

After the AI chipmaker Nvidia announced it was bringing back embattled former head Jensen Huang and the company's stock shot up like a bullet, President Donald Trump took a very public victory lap.

"I made the deal," he said during a lengthy phone interview with cable business news channel CNBC.

Trump followed that with an AI-generated image posted to his social media platform that riffed on the famous photograph taken moments after the 2024 attempt on his life in Pennsylvania. But instead of Trump in the image, Huang was the one surrounded by Secret Service guards. It depicted him in front of an Nvidia banner - with a raised first clenching a red bra.

The post was classic Trump – potentially offensive, yet still a bit opaque.

Was Trump suggesting Huang survived a scandal – one that includes allegations of recklessly jeopardising US national security by consorting with a suspected Chinese spy – the way he had survived an assassin's bullet?

Was the bra a celebration Huang's reported extramarital affairs? By replacing the US flag with an Nvidia standard, was he claiming that America and one of its largest, most powerful companies are one and the same?

At the very least, the image underscores how inextricably linked Huang and Trump now are, with the fate of the former hinging on the successes and failures of the latter.

Image source, Getty Images

And with that comes significant risks for the American president and for Republicans, including Vice-President JD Vance, who played a key part in his efforts to rescue Huang.

While Trump has said that a "very thorough investigation" by federal officials "exonerated" Huang and his reinstatement poses no national security threat, that is far from the final word on the matter.

"Every time you have a Chinese woman that's good looking or beautiful, they say she's a spy," Trump told CNBC, adding that "with Jensen, I don't believe that's true".

Democrats and some concerned Republicans in Congress have a different view.

They are promising to launch their own oversight of Huang and Nvidia, with subpoenas and compelled witness testimony, in order to assess whether they violated laws by allowing China to access sophisticated microchip technology.

State governments could also launch their own investigations.

Any new revelations could further damage the company's standing – and, by association, Trump himself.

"I have warned the administration from the start about Communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access," Republican Senator Tom Cotton posted on X.

"Congress has much to investigate," he said.

• Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone awayPublished12 hours ago

• What Jensen Huang's return teaches China's Xi about TrumpPublished23 hours ago

• US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigationPublished3 hours ago

While Huang has a long record of success at Nvidia, there is no guarantee that he can recapture past glory now that his star his dimmed.

Even if he is free from any criminal liability, the tech mogul is about to be in a much harsher spotlight than he has ever experienced.

Trump also appears to be on the wrong side of public opinion when it comes to AI writ large.

In the recent US midterm elections, candidates on both the left and right campaigned on imposing new restrictions on data centre construction, with many calling for new legal guardrails to prevent AI-fuelled economic and social disruption.

"Rather than addressing the American people's growing concerns about AI, this administration remains asleep at the wheel or willfully ignorant as our most advanced technologies fall into the hands of our greatest competitors," congresswoman Sydney Kamlager-Dove, a California Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, told the BBC.

The president's own political base is also suspicious of the new technology, with rural conservatives often rebelling at the demands that big tech companies have placed on their local resources and civic infrastructure.

Figure caption,

How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO

The Nvidia story has also exposed rifts in Trump's own administration, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, a China hawk, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, a vocal proponent of AI, publicly feuding over whether to impose new restrictions on AI chip exports.

Both Bessent and Lutnick travelled with Trump on his recent trip to China, although it was the commerce secretary who hitched a ride back to the White House on the Marine One helicopter when Trump returned to Washington last Thursday.

Polling also indicated that political corruption was a top issue for voters this year.

The president's willingness to intervene in the deliberations of a major private company in which he owns millions of dollars of stock could further fuel those concerns.

Trump's decision to help save Huang – noting on Monday that "we have to protect our geniuses, and he certainly is a genius" – could further inflame the public's sense that the rich and powerful, genius or not, play by a different set of rules.

"It almost feels like they've bent the rule, the regulation, to allow this to happen because it's such an important part of our economy right now," Steve Bannon, a former top Trump adviser, said on his podcast on Monday.

"Even in the crash of 2008... I never saw the government step in and take over a board of directors."

For this American president, however, these risks appear to be worth taking because of the stakes involved.

Trump has long viewed the success of the US economy as a key part of his political legacy.

He boasted of the historic growth and low unemployment during his first presidential term (while glossing over the disruptions caused by the Covid pandemic).

And since returning to office, he has celebrated as major US stock indices posted new record highs.

Recent US economic expansion has been fuelled largely by investment in AI technology, and Trump has become one of the industry's biggest boosters.

He scolded states and local governments for blocking data centre construction and predicted that the nation that wins the race for supremacy in AI – which he has tried to rebrand as "super intelligence" – will control the fate of the world.

If Trump views the economy as the key to his political success and AI as instrumental to the health of the US economy, then his dramatic, precedent-shattering actions to try to rescue Nvidia, the company at the centre of America's AI industry, make more sense.

In the weeks since concerns over Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy first surfaced, Nvidia's stock price tumbled more than 32%.

Last Friday alone, it fell 14%.

US stock indices tumbled as well, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq down 10% last week and the larger S&P 500 dropping 8.6%.

The recent financial turmoil may have given Trump a glimpse into a future where AI growth is just the latest financial bubble – like the housing market in 2008 and internet companies in 2001 – that is due for a resounding pop, with similarly dire economic consequences to follow.

Trump's intervention on behalf of Huang arrested that drop, at least for a day.

On Tuesday, Nvidia's stock price gave back much of the bounce it had enjoyed, and larger stock indices were mixed. The fate of the America economy and the AI juggernaut that has powered it is still undetermined.

Trump's intervention may not be a crisis fully averted, but only a crisis delayed.

And if an AI reckoning does come, the US president will be hard-pressed to avoid being caught in the maelstrom.

items.title: The rising cost of putting food on the table in India
items.summary: India's food inflation is broadening, squeezing household budgets.
items.body:
Image source, NurPhoto via Getty Images

Image caption,

As food inflation rises, vegetables are becoming an increasingly expensive part of the household budget

By

Soutik Biswas

India correspondent

India's inflation is rising again. And the biggest worry is what's happening to food prices.

The latest government data, external shows retail inflation climbed to 6.09% in October, up from 5.54% in September.

But look more closely at food inflation. It has surged to 8.94%.

The squeeze was sharper in rural India, where food inflation was 9.09%, compared with 8.68% in urban areas.

In other words, food prices are rising considerably faster than the overall rate of inflation.

Food inflation this year has been driven by a combination of weather disruptions, supply shortages and rising input costs, say economists.

With nearly 60% of its farmland dependent on rainfall, external, India remains acutely vulnerable to the vagaries of the monsoon. This year, the southwest monsoon was 13% below normal and unevenly distributed, while intensifying El Niño conditions have heightened risks to farm production.

Image source, Hindustan Times via Getty Images

Image caption,

Onion prices have surged, adding to the pressure on household food budgets

Food accounts for a smaller share of Indian household spending than it once did, but remains the biggest driver of inflation, with significant economic, social and political consequences.

In India's latest consumer price index, food and beverages account for 36.75% of the basket of goods and services used to measure inflation.

That is down sharply from 45.86% under the previous series, reflecting changing consumption patterns as Indians spend more on services, transport, healthcare, education and other non-food items.

Yet a sharp increase in food prices can move the overall inflation rate significantly, while disproportionately affecting people whose incomes leave little room for adjustment.

"Adjustability for a poor country like India is significantly lower," says Rajeswari Sengupta, an associate professor of economics at Mumbai-based Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, pointing to the fact that a substantial proportion of household income is still spent on food.

Image source, Hindustan Times via Getty Images

Image caption,

Rising food prices hurt the poor the most

The numbers bear this out.

According to calculations by Dharmakirti Joshi, chief economist at analytics firm Crisil, the bottom 20% of rural households faced inflation of 6.9% in October, against 6.5% for the richest 20%.

In urban India, the corresponding rates were 6.1% and 5.3%.

The pressure is visible even in the cost of a simple meal.

Crisil's Roti Rice Rate analysis, external found that the cost of a home-cooked vegetarian thali - a meal platter - rose 12% year-on-year in October, driven by higher prices of onions, tomatoes, vegetables, edible oil, rice and cooking gas. A non-vegetarian thali became 9% more expensive.

Rice prices were up about 10% year-on-year, pulses 8%, edible oil 13% and LPG 10%, according to Pushan Sharma, director of intelligence at Crisil. "It's no longer a few commodities that are driving this increase, it's becoming a little more broad-based," he says.

When onion prices spike, households can cut back on their consumption to some extent. But substituting rice, pulses and cooking oil is considerably harder.

And food inflation is not just about what farmers produce. It is also about how efficiently that food is stored, processed and moved to the market. Weaknesses at each stage can turn seasonal shortages into sharp price spikes - and gluts into waste.

• Onionomics: Peeling away the layers of India's food economy

Onions, for instance, are particularly susceptible to seasonal price swings.

The rabi crop - winter crops, sown after the monsoon and harvested in spring - which accounts for roughly two-thirds of onion production, is harvested in March and April and stored for several months. As stocks dwindle, prices can rise sharply before the next crop arrives.

Tomatoes, meanwhile, tend to see price spikes during the summer months, when arrivals decline in some markets or heat stress affects production.

Sharma says perishables are often responsible for the sudden spikes in food inflation, while prices of staples such as rice and wheat tend to rise more gradually but can stay higher for longer.

"The perishables are what caused the volatility. The non-perishables, like rice and wheat, are the ones that structurally increase the cost," he says.

Economists say India still lacks adequate infrastructure to sort, grade, store and process much of its perishable produce.

Tomatoes, for example, can become so abundant during a glut that farmers struggle to sell them at remunerative prices, only for consumers to face sharply higher prices months later.

Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images

Image caption,

With nearly 60% of its farmland dependent on rainfall, India remains vulnerable to erratic monsoons

Better storage and processing could help turn some of that surplus into products such as puree, smoothing the extremes between abundance and scarcity, according to Sharma

There are other pressures.

Energy shocks feed into the cost of transport, irrigation and agricultural inputs. Fertiliser prices can rise. Global edible-oil markets matter because India relies heavily on imports.

To be true, India, however, has some protection against the worst effects of food inflation.

Government stocks of cereals are comfortably above prescribed minimum levels, and the free-food programme covering nearly 800 million people offers a cushion against rising prices. Rice stocks, external are particularly ample.

There is a wider economic risk, says Sengupta.

"Food inflation may begin with a supply shock, but its effects can spread. Workers who find that their wages no longer cover basic living costs may seek higher pay. Businesses facing higher labour costs may raise prices. What begins as a rise in the price of food can gradually become a more general inflationary pressure - the familiar wage-price spiral that central banks try to prevent," she says.

For India, this creates a particularly difficult balancing act.

Agriculture is a relatively low-productivity sector, and the government has long sought to protect farmers by setting minimum support prices (MSPs) for certain crops - a price floor at which it promises to buy produce, helping farmers guard against a market crash.

Image source, Robert Nickelsberg/Getty Images

Image caption,

India has ample buffer food stocks

At the same time, food prices are politically sensitive. Sharp increases in the price of staples such as onions and tomatoes can quickly anger consumers, prompting governments to step in with measures such as restricting exports, limiting how much traders can stockpile, or otherwise trying to bring prices down.

The broader story of India's changing food consumption makes the current inflation more interesting.

Households are eating differently from a decade ago. An analysis, external of the 2011-12 and 2023-24 consumption surveys shows that the share of cereals in food spending has fallen sharply, particularly among the poorest households, reflecting the impact of subsidised food programmes.

Meanwhile, consumption of nutrient-rich foods such as dairy, fruit and meat has increased across income groups, with the biggest gains among the poorest, the study revealed.

India's food basket is becoming more diverse. But diversity is meaningful only if ordinary Indians can afford it. Ultimately, food inflation is about what makes it to the plate - and what has to be left out.

Rice prices were up about 10% year-on-year, pulses 8%, edible oil 13% and LPG 10%, according to Pushan Sharma, director of intelligence at Crisil. "It's no longer a few commodities that are driving this increase, it's becoming a little more broad-based," he says.
When onion prices spike, households can cut back on their consumption to some extent. But substituting rice, pulses and cooking oil is considerably harder.

And food inflation is not just about what farmers produce. It is also about how efficiently that food is stored, processed and moved to the market. Weaknesses at each stage can turn seasonal shortages into sharp price spikes - and gluts into waste.

items: Onionomics: Peeling away the layers of India's food economy

blocks.text: Onions, for instance, are particularly susceptible to seasonal price swings.

The rabi crop - winter crops, sown after the monsoon and harvested in spring - which accounts for roughly two-thirds of onion production, is harvested in March and April and stored for several months. As stocks dwindle, prices can rise sharply before the next crop arrives.
Tomatoes, meanwhile, tend to see price spikes during the summer months, when arrivals decline in some markets or heat stress affects production.
Sharma says perishables are often responsible for the sudden spikes in food inflation, while prices of staples such as rice and wheat tend to rise more gradually but can stay higher for longer.
"The perishables are what caused the volatility. The non-perishables, like rice and wheat, are the ones that structurally increase the cost," he says.
Economists say India still lacks adequate infrastructure to sort, grade, store and process much of its perishable produce.
Tomatoes, for example, can become so abundant during a glut that farmers struggle to sell them at remunerative prices, only for consumers to face sharply higher prices months later.

blocks.alt: Farmers at a flooded rice paddy field on the outskirts of Mumbai, India

blocks.text: Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images
Image caption,
With nearly 60% of its farmland dependent on rainfall, India remains vulnerable to erratic monsoons
Better storage and processing could help turn some of that surplus into products such as puree, smoothing the extremes between abundance and scarcity, according to Sharma
There are other pressures.
Energy shocks feed into the cost of transport, irrigation and agricultural inputs. Fertiliser prices can rise. Global edible-oil markets matter because India relies heavily on imports.
To be true, India, however, has some protection against the worst effects of food inflation.

Government stocks of cereals are comfortably above prescribed minimum levels, and the free-food programme covering nearly 800 million people offers a cushion against rising prices. Rice stocks, external are particularly ample.
There is a wider economic risk, says Sengupta.

"Food inflation may begin with a supply shock, but its effects can spread. Workers who find that their wages no longer cover basic living costs may seek higher pay. Businesses facing higher labour costs may raise prices. What begins as a rise in the price of food can gradually become a more general inflationary pressure - the familiar wage-price spiral that central banks try to prevent," she says.
For India, this creates a particularly difficult balancing act.

Agriculture is a relatively low-productivity sector, and the government has long sought to protect farmers by setting minimum support prices (MSPs) for certain crops - a price floor at which it promises to buy produce, helping farmers guard against a market crash.

blocks.alt: India food stocks

blocks.text: Image source, Robert Nickelsberg/Getty Images
Image caption,
India has ample buffer food stocks

At the same time, food prices are politically sensitive. Sharp increases in the price of staples such as onions and tomatoes can quickly anger consumers, prompting governments to step in with measures such as restricting exports, limiting how much traders can stockpile, or otherwise trying to bring prices down.
The broader story of India's changing food consumption makes the current inflation more interesting.

Households are eating differently from a decade ago. An analysis, external of the 2011-12 and 2023-24 consumption surveys shows that the share of cereals in food spending has fallen sharply, particularly among the poorest households, reflecting the impact of subsidised food programmes.
Meanwhile, consumption of nutrient-rich foods such as dairy, fruit and meat has increased across income groups, with the biggest gains among the poorest, the study revealed.

India's food basket is becoming more diverse. But diversity is meaningful only if ordinary Indians can afford it. Ultimately, food inflation is about what makes it to the plate - and what has to be left out.
